prize_parts.citation: For a body of poetry, essay and hybrid narrative that renews literary form through a living dialogue with antiquity, joining erudition, wit and elegiac feeling.

statement.case_for: Carson has one of the most recognisable voices on the shortlist. She joins classical learning, lyric, essay, verse-novel and book-object form without letting the apparatus smother feeling. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a contemporary verse novel, and Nox turns elegy into an archival object. From public knowledge, the essays and shorter lyric collections show the same intelligence at the level of the sentence and the line, so the case does not rest on two famous books. The achievement is formal, linguistic and intellectual at once. It also fits the idealistic direction of Nobel's will in its insistence on the human capacity for love, grief and understanding across two millennia. After reading colleagues' arguments I still rank her first, but by a narrower margin than in my opening. The reasons are the scope and durability questions raised below, which I take seriously and answer only partly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is whether the oeuvre has a durable central core or is a series of brilliant experiments. Part of the effect depends on scholarly apparatus, classical knowledge and book design, which may not survive other editions or translation. Her translations and adaptations of Greek texts complicate what counts as her own creative corpus. A citation would have to define the scope with care. Cărtărescu offers a more monumental, sustained architecture, and Can Xue a more radical estrangement of narrative itself. Against either, Carson's case may look more compact and more dependent on English-language and academic readership.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson fifth. She admires Carson's wit, erudition and formal invention. She asks how far translations of ancient texts belong to the creative oeuvre, and whether the career has a central durable core or a series of brilliant experiments.
responses.response: I accept that the translation question is real, and I would write the citation so that it rests on the original poetry, essays and verse-novel forms and treats the translations as context. On durability, I read the recurring concerns as a core: desire, loss, the pull of the classical text, and the fragment as a unit of thought. They return across her essays, her lyric sequences and Nox, in changing forms. That makes them a method rather than a string of one-off experiments. I cannot fully prove this from general public knowledge, and I have not verified the later volumes. I would therefore want the committee to test it against the whole bibliography before relying on it.

responses.point: Olsson puts Can Xue first for a singular, sustained, anti-realist voice. On Carson he asks whether her experiments rest on scholarly and book-design effects that are less stable than sustained achievement in language, and he notes that later work may be occasional or performance-oriented.
responses.response: The book-design point carries weight for Nox, which is partly an object. But the verse-novel, the essays and the shorter lyrics work on the page as language, so the claim does not depend on layout alone. I agree that some later pieces are more occasional, and that counts against uniform quality. Can Xue's case is a serious one. Her method is consistent and unmistakable, but I share the concern raised by Palm and Sem-Sandberg that a very stable method may mean limited range. Neither of us can judge the sentence-level texture in translation, so I would not use that as the deciding point.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He credits her unmistakable voice and line-level quality but says her compact, formally varied corpus makes uniform depth harder to assess than for a large novelistic oeuvre. He also wonders how she relates to the 'idealistic direction'.
responses.response: I agree that depth is easier to test in a large oeuvre than in a varied, compact one, and this is why Cărtărescu remains my first alternative. I would not equate scale with depth, though. A compact corpus that is formally varied and still coherent can show sustained quality, and Carson's range is part of the achievement. On the idealistic direction, I read it through the elegiac and ethical seriousness of her treatment of love, memory and loss, not through any programme. I accept that this reading is arguable.

responses.point: Palm also ranks Carson first, but flags that the hybrid forms may be judged either as a sustained achievement or as a narrowly appealing erudite mode, and that the translations are hard to separate from her own voice.
responses.response: Palm's formulation seems right to me, and it is the crux. That we both ranked her first should not count as an argument for her. My answer is that the hybrid forms recur and develop across decades, and that is evidence of a sustained achievement rather than a mode. The unseparated translation question is best handled by a citation that names poetry, essay and hybrid narrative and does not mention translation as a ground.

uncertainties: My assessment rests on general public knowledge of the main volumes. I have not independently verified texts, and coverage of the recent work is uncertain.
Whether the hybrid, fragmentary and book-object forms count as sustained literary achievement or as an erudite mode with narrower significance is a judgment on which members could reasonably differ.
How far her translations and adaptations of classical texts belong to the creative oeuvre affects the citation scope and is unresolved.
Translation coverage of her work beyond English is uncertain, and so is her significance outside English-language and academic readerships.

Cărtărescu's case may be stronger on sustained scale, but I cannot assess the Romanian prose or its translations. The comparison between the two cases therefore depends on how the committee weighs monumental architecture against formal range.
My simulated vote rests on the modelling assumption that a co-opted member votes. Her actual voting status is undocumented.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. As Permanent Secretary, a Swedish Academy member and a co-opted committee member of uncertain voting status, she has no documented connection to any shortlisted writer. Her marriage and her biographical work on Raoul Wallenberg and Alfred Nobel are not connected to any shortlisted writer.
